newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Air NZ on brink of Ansett purchase.
newsitem.headline: Air NZ on brink of Ansett purchase.

text.p: Air New Zealand on Monday appeared quietly confident that its long-running bid to gain access to Australian skies by buying half of Ansett Airlines would soon become a reality.

Air NZ Chairman Bob Matthew, speaking at a news conference after the company's annual result, said he had hoped also to make an announcement on the planned purchase of 50 percent of Ansett from TNT Ltd.

"I'm afraid to say that we are still not in a position to make an announcement on our proposed investment in Ansett Australia, but you should not be surprised if later today or early tomorrow we give you a call and invite you over for another briefing," Matthew said.

Matthew declined to comment on how the purchase, which has yet to gain approval from Australia's Foreign Investment Review Board, would be funded. Analysts estimate the half share is worth around NZ$300-400 million.
Air NZ earlier reported a 13.4 percent decline in profit to NZ$225.2 million, which was the company's second highest profit.
Directors said it would be difficult to match that outcome in the current year and analysts said this went some way to highlight the need Air NZ had for Ansett, if it wanted to keep on growing.
Matthew said the result was not as good as he had expected but still represented a 16 percent return on shareholders funds.
The strong New Zealand dollar, a slowing in tourism growth and increased competition were behind the decline.
Matthew said the strong currency cost about NZ$100 million in revenue. Countering that was a reduction in costs, giving a net cost effect of about $40 million.
Managing Director Jim McCrea said the company's rapid network expansion over the last five years was now at an end and that it would concentrate on consolidation.
Over the year, international capacity rose by 16.5 percent and had doubled over the last five years.
"We think we've got the network right internationally and reasonably well organised domestically," he said.
McCrea said he did not expect to see a lot of fleet acquisitions this year or the coming year while the company consolidated.

"That's the last of the rapid and big growth of Air New Zealand for some time. That's the network in place so in future we will be filling in the gaps and lifting the frequency as market competition requires or as market growth allows."
Matthew said world economies were not in bad shape and that continued growth in aviation markets could therefore be expected, particularly in the Asia-Pacific region.

"It would be prudent for us to assume that competition is something that is going to heighten rather than lessen. That does not hold special fears for us but it nevertheless is something that needs to be acknowleged and one needs to
pragmatically address and take account of in our stategies."
Domestically, either low growth or no growth at all was possible over the next 12 months but Australia probably held more promise in terms of expansion.
Air NZ targeted savings of NZ$100 million, most of which would not take effect until the second half.
Asked to comment on cut price operator Kiwi International, which is fighting for its survival, Matthew said Kiwi was but one of 23 international competitors, most of whom were far more important.
Air NZ's own cut-price unit, Freedom Air, made a small loss but is expected to be close to profit in financial 1996/7.
-- Wellington Newsroom (64-4-4734746)
